title: Design and verify: a new scheme for generating cutting-planes
contribution: Introduces verification closures (accept a designed integer inequality if a black-box cut procedure empties its reverse half-space), proves they are almost admissible, places them in the hierarchy of GC, split and matrix-cut closures, and gives rank bounds showing they are strong but not unrealistically so (read as the November 2010 draft).
problem_entry: Generic cuts are produced 'almost blindly' to separate the current fractional point; ask how much stronger a cut family is when the black box only verifies a designed inequality instead of computing it (p. 2).
key_idea: V-closure ∂M(P) = intersection of integer inequalities cx <= d with M(P ∩ {cx >= d+1}) empty; strength comes from M(P ∩ {cx >= d+1}) ⊆ M(P) ∩ {cx >= d+1} (eqs. (1)-(2), p. 2; Example 1, p. 3).
assumptions: M admissible in the Pokutta-Schulz axiomatic sense (Def. 2.1, p. 4); rational polytopes, mostly in [0,1]^n.
proof_devices: Axiomatic transfer: ∂M satisfies all admissibility axioms except short verification, strong homogeneity via tilting by a face inequality (Thm 2.3, Lemma 2.2, pp. 4-5)
Support-function comparison over integer directions only (Lemma 3.2, Thm 3.3, pp. 5-6)
Coordinate rounding gives ∂M ⊆ GC and ∂M ⊆ N0 for every admissible M (Thm 3.4, p. 6)
One-coordinate padding turns a separating example into non-refinement of V-closures (Prop. 3.7, p. 7)
Rank lower bounds inherited from the base operator on A_n and the TSP relaxation (Thm 4.3, Cor 4.4, p. 9; Thm 5.5, p. 11)
Maximal lattice-free triangles show ∂GC(P) = P_I in the plane (Thm 5.6, p. 11)
positioning: Builds on the admissible-closure framework of Pokutta-Schulz [19]; only related idea cited is Cook-Coullard-Turan [4] (p. 2).
writing: Paradigm stated in two sentences on p. 2; results summarized by a refinement diagram (Fig. 1, p. 6); conclusion pairs 'very strong' with 'not unrealistically strong' (p. 11); many proofs deferred to a full version (pp. 4, 6).
limits_future: No algorithm for designing candidate inequalities and no computation; proofs deferred to the full version (pp. 4, 6, 11).

method_links.note: Strength results paired with lower bounds (A_n rank, TSP Θ(n)) and a matching upper bound for A_n
Starts from a solver habit (blind black-box cut generation) but proposes a new paradigm instead of explaining the habit

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Results proved once for every admissible operator, covering GC, split, N0, N, N+ together

transferable: Prove comparisons of a new closure inside an axiom system so one theorem covers all classical closures (Thm 3.4, p. 6)
Show a new operator is not unrealistically strong by rerunning the standard hard families (A_n, TSP) and inheriting the base operator's lower bound (pp. 9, 11)

quotes.text: First we design a useful cutting-plane without considering its validity. Then, once the cutting-plane is designed, we verify whether it is valid.
On the other hand, we also show that the verification scheme is not unrealistically strong, as illustrated by Theorem 4.3 and Theorem 5.5.

title: Two dimensional lattice-free cuts and asymmetric disjunctions for mixed-integer polyhedra
contribution: Introduces cross and crooked cross (asymmetric 2-branch split) cuts and shows that for the two-row canonical set unimodular cross cuts equal non-type-3 lattice-free cuts and crooked cross cuts give the hull, while for general MIPs every (crooked) cross cut comes from a three-row relaxation (two-row for full-row-rank A).
problem_entry: Relate two cut strands, intersection cuts from 2D maximal lattice-free sets and t-branch split disjunctions, and seek the analogue of 'split cut = MIR cut from a one-row relaxation' (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Q = UC and CC = Q ∩ T3 = conv(W) for the two-row set (Thm 3.1, p. 7); type 3 triangles are not in any cross set (Lemma 3.3, p. 7); any (crooked) cross cut is a cut of a three-row relaxation up to translation (Thm 5.8, p. 25), two-row when A has full row rank (Cor 5.9, p. 26).
assumptions: Rational mixed-integer polyhedra Ax + Gy = b, y >= 0 (p. 3); canonical two-row set with free integer basics and continuous nonbasics (p. 1).
proof_devices: Unimodular transformation to standard form, then containment of lattice-free sets in a union of two splits (Lemma 3.2, p. 7)
Contradiction from integer points in the relative interior of triangle sides (Lemma 3.3, p. 7)
A cross cut is a split cut for each of two half-space restrictions; reuse the three-case split = MIR proof (p. 18)
positioning: Extends Andersen-Louveaux-Weismantel-Wolsey, Cornuéjols-Margot, Li-Richard and Balas (2009); generalizes Nemhauser-Wolsey's split = MIR equivalence (pp. 1-2).
writing: Main result framed as an '(approximately) analogous result' to the one-row case (p. 2); open problems listed in the conclusion with stated beliefs (p. 27).
limits_future: Strict dominance of crooked cross over 2D lattice-free cuts unproved; polyhedrality of the closures open; whether crooked cross cuts give the hull with two integer variables conjectured; choosing good disjunctions computationally hard and untested (pp. 14, 27).

method_links.note: MILP-internal precursor: a known one-row equivalence lifted to two-branch disjunctions and multi-row relaxations
Equivalences come with what fails (type 3 triangles) and explicit open strictness questions

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: lift a known equivalence one dimension up
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: split = 1D lattice-free (MIR) cut generalized to (crooked) cross cut = cut from a three-row relaxation, with the same case analysis

transferable: Generalize a classical equivalence by redoing its case analysis literally and matching the new cases to the old ones (p. 18)
State conjectured strictness as a belief and an open problem (pp. 14, 27)

quotes.text: Even though we believe this dominance to be strict, we are not able to establish it.
It seems hard to devise an effective algorithm to find good, maximal, lattice-free bodies such that the associated cuts are violated by the current LP solution.

title: A strong dual for conic mixed-integer programs
contribution: Extends the subadditive dual of MILP to mixed-integer conic programs (subadditive functions nondecreasing with respect to the cone) and proves strong duality when a mixed-integer point lies strictly inside the conic constraint, a condition shown by examples to be essential.
problem_entry: The MILP subadditive dual is well understood; can it be extended to mixed-integer conic programs (pp. 1-2)?
key_idea: Dual (D) over subadditive, K-nondecreasing functions with column conditions; recovers the MILP dual for K = R^m_+; strong duality under an interior mixed-integer point, which replaces rational data (Thm 2.4, pp. 2-3).
assumptions: K closed, pointed, full-dimensional cone (p. 2); condition (∗): a mixed-integer x̂ with Ax̂ strictly inside K-feasibility (p. 3).
proof_devices: Three proof ingredients announced up front: finiteness equivalence with the continuous relaxation, conic strong duality, value-function construction (p. 1)
Finiteness equivalence via maximal lattice-free convex sets (Thm 4.3, Cor 4.4, Prop. 4.5, pp. 5-6)
Subadditive 0/1 feasibility indicator G so that g + λG is dual feasible and unbounded when the primal is infeasible (Prop. 5.1, p. 9)
Dual-optimal g* built from the value function by a sign case analysis (Prop. 5.3, pp. 10-12)
positioning: Generalizes the MILP subadditive dual as presented in §II.3.3 of [11] (p. 2); relies on strong duality for conic programming (§4.2, p. 6).
writing: Main theorem stated in §2 before any proof (p. 3); each hypothesis is followed by a counterexample (pp. 4-6).
limits_future: Interior condition crucial (Examples 4.1-4.2, pp. 4-6); a finite family of dual functions as in pure IP unlikely because hulls need not be polyhedral (Example 6.2, p. 12); no tractability claim.

method_links.note: Direct instance of the 'Dual ?' item: MILP subadditive duality generalized to the conic class, MILP case recovered
Counterexamples show the interior condition cannot be dropped; converse of Prop. 4.5 refuted

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Interior mixed-integer point plays the role of rational data in the strong-duality proof

transferable: List the classical theorem's proof ingredients in the introduction and generalize each one separately (p. 1)
Give a small 2D/3D counterexample for each hypothesis of a generalized theorem (Examples 4.1, 4.2, p. 4)
coauthors: Diego A. Morán R., Juan Pablo Vielma

quotes.text: Condition (∗) in the case of mixed-integer conic programs plays the same role as the assumption of rational data in the case of mixed-integer programs in the proof of the strong duality result.
The condition that there exists a mixed-integer feasible solution in the interior of the continuous relaxation is crucial for Proposition 4.5.

title: Forbidding extreme points from the 0-1 hypercube
contribution: Gives an extended formulation of size O(mn) for the convex hull of the 0-1 hypercube minus a list of m points, via binary expansion and a two-sided generalization of the Laurent-Sassano hull of superincreasing knapsacks.
problem_entry: Is there a description of conv({0,1}^n \ V), V a list of m points, polynomial in n and m (p. 1)?
key_idea: Binary expansion writes {0,1}^n \ V as a union of m+1 interval sets K(a, b); the two-sided superincreasing knapsack hull is the intersection of the cover and reverse-cover hulls (Thm 2, p. 3); Balas' disjunctive union gives the extended formulation (pp. 2, 8).
assumptions: V given explicitly; superincreasing weights (Def. 1, p. 2).
proof_devices: Induction on n with three cases on w_n against a and b (pp. 3-4)
Disjunctive hull of the x_n = 0 and x_n = 1 pieces followed by variable-by-variable Fourier-Motzkin projection, with a claim fixing every intermediate polyhedron (pp. 5-7)
positioning: Generalizes Laurent-Sassano [3]; uses Balas' disjunctive programming [1]; notes independent work by Muldoon-Adams-Sherali [4] (footnote, p. 1).
writing: Eight-page note: question, one-line answer with size, proof (p. 1).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated; priority shared with Muldoon et al. (p. 1).

method_links.note: Step 4: constructive proof with an explicit extended formulation whose size O(mn) is the headline

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry the induction through a projection
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Hull proved by disjunctive lifting plus Fourier-Motzkin elimination with a claim on each intermediate projection

transferable: Turn 'forbid a list of points' into a union of intervals in an encoding order (binary expansion) and take the disjunctive hull of the pieces (p. 2)
Prove a hull by induction via the disjunctive hull of two fixings and coordinate-wise elimination, stating each intermediate projection as a claim (pp. 5-7)

quotes.text: Is it possible to give a description of conv(B \ V ) which is polynomial in n and m?
Our approach relies on being able to give the convex hull of binary knapsack sets having a superincreasing weight.

title: Some properties of convex hulls of integer points contained in general convex sets
contribution: Characterizes when the convex hull of integer points in a closed convex set is closed, and shows that thinness plus a rational polyhedral recession cone is sufficient (and, with an interior integer point, necessary) for it to be a polyhedron, generalizing Meyer's theorem.
problem_entry: Meyer's theorem relies on Minkowski-Weyl and rational recession cones, unavailable for general convex K; even closedness of conv(K ∩ Z^n) is not well understood (p. 2).
key_idea: Closed iff u(K) is the same at all integer points, for line-free K (Thm 1, p. 3), with refinements (Thms 2-5, pp. 3-4); 'thin' sets (Def. 2, p. 4) + rational polyhedral recession cone ⇒ polyhedral hull, converse with an interior integer point (Thm 6, p. 4).
assumptions: K closed convex; int(K) ∩ Z^n non-empty for the necessity parts (Thm 2, Thm 6, pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: Gallery of planar examples separating candidate explanations before the theorems (Example 1, pp. 4-5)
Gordan-Dickson-type finiteness lemma in the polyhedrality proof (Lemma 11, p. 17)
Maximal lattice-free convex sets (Thm 8, p. 7; not read in detail)
positioning: Generalizes Meyer [8] and the closedness conditions of [9] for non-rational polyhedra (p. 2); contrasts with integral generating sets [4] (p. 2).
writing: All main results collected in §2 before the proofs (pp. 3-4); each technical condition shown 'not artificial' by an example (pp. 10, 20).
limits_future: Open: necessary and sufficient conditions for local polyhedrality and for solvability of linear optimization over K ∩ Z^n (pp. 20-21).

method_links.note: Generalizes the MILP structure theorem (Meyer) to convex integer sets, naming which ingredient survives and what must be added
Each hypothesis shown necessary by an explicit example; sufficient condition also necessary under an interior integer point

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Thin set + rational polyhedral recession cone replaces rational data in Meyer's theorem

transferable: Show a gallery of small planar examples separating candidate explanations before stating the theorems (pp. 4-5)
Split a structural question into a weaker necessary property (closedness) and the strong one (polyhedrality) (p. 2)

quotes.text: In the world of mixed integer linear programming (MILP) problems, these sufficient conditions for polyhedrality of the convex hull of feasible solutions are reasonable since we expect most instances to be described using rational data.
We note here that the condition that K contains no line in the statement of Theorem 1 is not artificial.

title: Semi-continuous network flow problems
contribution: Introduces the semi-continuous inflow set with variable upper bounds as a relaxation of semi-continuous network flows, gives complete hull descriptions and extended formulations for two special cases, proves complexity results for a semi-continuous transportation problem, and shows the cuts speed up CPLEX, best in a binary formulation.
problem_entry: Semi-continuous flows arise in inventory, portfolio, petrochemical and supply-chain models; binary modelling enlarges problems but enables presolve (pp. 1-2); take the node inflow substructure as a relaxation (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: NP-hardness of the substructure (Prop. 1, p. 4), then hulls and extended formulations for t = 0 (Thm 6, p. 8; Cor 9, p. 11) and h = 0 (Thm 15, p. 15; Prop. 17, p. 17); transportation version NP-hard (Prop. 18, p. 19) but polynomial for fixed m when h = 0 (Thm 21, p. 24; Cor 22, p. 25).
assumptions: Unbounded semi-continuous variables; big-M bound M = max{d̄, l̄, h̄} + t̄ in the binary formulation (p. 25).
proof_devices: Knapsack reduction (Prop. 1, p. 4) and UFLP reduction (Prop. 18, p. 19) for NP-hardness
Hull completeness: for every objective, all optimal solutions lie on one listed facet (Thm 6, p. 8)
Extreme-point support counting by convex-combination splitting (Prop. 19, p. 21; Thm 21, p. 24)
experiments: Random semi-continuous transportation instances, n, m in {30, 50, 80}, 10 each; CPLEX 12.2 default vs own root cuts vs both vs extended formulation, in semi-continuous and binary models, 1,800 s, single thread; own cuts alone in the binary model fastest and the only way to solve the largest instances (pp. 25-29, Tables 1-8).
positioning: Extends the semi-continuous knapsack cuts of [6, 7] and branching without binaries [4, 5] to network flows (p. 2).
writing: Contribution paragraph on p. 2; surprises flagged in the computation ('may be a bit surprising', p. 26; p. 27).
limits_future: Fixed-m algorithm inapplicable in practice (p. 25); extended formulation for t > 0 too large (p. 26); binary formulation wins, probably due to CPLEX bound tightening (p. 29). Future: finite upper bounds, simultaneous inflows and outflows (p. 29).

method_links.note: Recurring node substructure cut out as a relaxation, convexified jointly, returned to a testbed
NP-hardness of substructure and transportation problem, tractable fixed-m boundary, with its practical irrelevance stated
No exact ceiling; the extended formulation arm serves as the all-cuts-present reference against CPLEX defaults

transferable: Test a cut family in both the native and the binary-reformulated model; report if the binary model wins because of solver presolve (pp. 27, 29)
Include the substructure's extended formulation as an arm next to on-the-fly separation (p. 26)

quotes.text: However, our experimental experience indicates that a standard branch-and-cut solver does not need to branch that many times, rendering this approach inapplicable for practical purposes.
In fact, applying these cuts to a binary formulation of such problems turned out to be the most effective method.

title: On the transportation problem with market choice
contribution: Shows the transportation problem with market choice is strongly NP-complete (demands 3) but polynomial with demands at most 2 (matching, blossom hull), derives valid inequalities and coefficient-update schemes for its cover and knapsack-with-VUB substructures with facet conditions, and reports preliminary branch-and-cut gains.
problem_entry: A capacitated transportation problem in which suppliers may reject markets, the less studied 'complement' of capacitated facility location (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Complexity boundary at demand 2 vs 3 (Props 1-2, p. 3); TPMC inequality (5) (Prop. 3, p. 4); coefficient-update schemes for a mixed-integer cover set (Prop. 4, pp. 4-5) and a knapsack with variable upper bounds (Prop. 5, p. 7); facet conditions (Thm 1, p. 9).
assumptions: Integral data; markets with demand above total supply pre-rejected, assumption (23) (p. 9).
proof_devices: Validity by case split on whether a large market is rejected (Prop. 3, p. 4)
Minimal-cover arguments for coefficient update (Prop. 4, pp. 4-5)
Necessary facet conditions each shown by implication from other inequalities (Thm 1, pp. 9-10)
Reductions from Exact 3-Cover and to minimum weight perfect matching (p. 3; Appendix, not read)
experiments: CPLEX 12.4, 8 size settings x 3 instances kept only if default CPLEX needs at least 15 min, 30 min limit; default vs default plus each user-cut family; root and end gap, time, unsolved, nodes; root gap barely changes, end gap and unsolved count drop, best with ≥-type cuts alone (pp. 23-25, Table 1).
positioning: Contrasts with CFL polyhedral work and with market-choice approximation algorithms for uncapacitated settings (p. 2); notes lifted flow cover and submodular inequalities also apply (p. 7).
writing: Preliminary nature of the computation stated in the introduction (p. 3) and repeated at the end (pp. 25-26).
limits_future: No extensive computational study; separation heuristic needs significant improvement (p. 3); type (9) cuts never generated on the test instances, with the reason (p. 25).

method_links.note: Relax to small mixed-integer substructures (cover set, knapsack with VUBs), derive inequalities there, lift back
Sharp complexity boundary at demand 2 vs 3; facet conditions split into necessary and sufficient parts

transferable: Draw the complexity boundary on one parameter before polyhedral work; the tractable side may come with a known hull (p. 3)
Make random instances hard by rejection sampling on default-solver time and say so in the setup (p. 23)
Add each user-cut family as its own arm next to all user cuts and the default (Table 1, pp. 24-25)

quotes.text: Therefore, we found “hard” instances by continually generating and solving instances until we were able to find 3 that were solved in at least 15 minutes under default CPLEX settings.
However, we do not give an extensive computational study and the heuristic separation we use needs significant improvement.

title: Some lower bounds on sparse outer approximations of polytopes
contribution: Shows by four lower-bound theorems that sparse cuts can approximate integer hulls badly even with an LP relaxation present, with exponentially many dense cuts added, after any rotation, and along almost every objective direction (read as arXiv:1412.3765v1).
problem_entry: Solvers bias cut selection toward sparse cuts; the earlier sparse-cut paper was 'idealized'; ask four 'less idealized' questions that restore features of practice (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Use simple polytopes P_{t,n} and the Hausdorff distance d(P, P^k) (= worst directional gap, Lemma 1) to prove Ω(√n) errors in all four settings (Thms 5-8, pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Polytopes in [0,1]^n or [-1,1]^n; k up to n/100, n/2003 or n/10 by theorem; constants not optimized (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: Explicit IP formulation Q_n whose LP point (n/(n+2))e is far from the hull (Thm 5, p. 4)
Random ±1 point scaled by 2/3; each dense cut split into its k largest coefficients plus a remainder bounded by Bernstein's inequality; union bound over exp(n/6002) cuts (Thm 6, pp. 5-6)
Polar duality with few-facet approximations of k-dimensional symmetric bodies to reduce rotations to the dense-cut theorem (Lemma 13, Thm 7, pp. 6-7)
Gaussian concentration of Lipschitz functions for random directions (Thm 16, Thm 8, p. 8)
positioning: Extension of their own sparse-cut paper [2]; tools from convex geometry and concentration of measure (pp. 1, 5, 8).
writing: Four numbered questions in the introduction answered by four theorems in one 'Main results' section before the proofs (pp. 1-4); outcome called 'perhaps not surprising' (p. 2).
limits_future: Open: when sparse inequalities are effective in these realistic settings (p. 2); examples are specific symmetric polytopes, not solver instances (my reading).

method_links.note: Solver habit (sparse-cut bias) studied through a geometric proxy, pushed toward realism one feature at a time
The paper demarcates the positive results of [2] with four lower bounds

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: de-idealize the proxy one realism at a time
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Four numbered questions each restore one feature of solver practice (LP relaxation, dense cuts, rotation, objective direction)

transferable: After an idealized positive result, write numbered follow-up questions each restoring one feature of practice (pp. 1-2)
To show a budget of arbitrary cuts cannot help: random bad point, split each cut into sparse part plus dense remainder, concentrate the remainder, union-bound (pp. 5-6)

quotes.text: In practice, however, most state-of-the-art IP solvers bias their cutting-plane selection towards the use of sparse inequalities.
This is perhaps not surprising: an indication that sparse inequalities do not always approximate integer hulls well even in the more realistic settings considered in this paper.
